paras: The stoning of the Barred home on Mosher Street was an attack in July 1919 in which whites threw stones and bricks through the windows of a house newly occupied by a Black family, Mr. and Mrs. James Barred. No one was hurt, and after a crowd that included Black soldiers in uniform gathered and the whites withdrew, one white man and two Black men were arrested. The Baltimore Afro-American reported it as a reaction to Black families buying homes in the block.

The Barreds had just moved into a two-story house at 1215 Mosher Street, printed as "Mooder street" in the body of the report. According to the Afro-American, the house was one of several in the block recently purchased by Arthur L. Johnson, and other "colored families" were moving there. The report does not name the city in which the street lay.

A little after ten o'clock on a Wednesday night, probably July 9, after the Barreds had retired, stones and bricks thrown by whites shattered the ground-floor window panes and struck the front of the second story. None of the missiles entered the upstairs windows, and no one was injured. By the time the couple came downstairs, the street had filled with white and Black people, "including many colored soldiers in uniform." Facing that crowd, the whites retreated, while Black men threatened to "skin them alive" if more bricks were thrown.

One white man and two Black men were arrested for disorderly conduct; the item does not say who made the arrests. No report of court proceedings or of further attacks on the house was found in the coverage.

The only report found ran in the Baltimore Afro-American on July 11, 1919, on page 5 under the headline "Stone Mosher Street Home." Its subhead emphasized Black resolve rather than the damage, announcing that "irate colored neighbors" threatened to retaliate "unless peace is made." The paper treated the stoning as a neighborhood story, tying it to the move-in and to the Black soldiers in uniform who turned out.
